      <h1 id="awesome-ai-coding-sandboxes-">Awesome AI Coding Sandboxes <a href="https://awesome.re"><img src="https://awesome.re/badge.svg" alt="Awesome" /></a></h1>

<blockquote>
  <p>A curated list of sandboxing and isolation solutions for running the code of autonomous <strong>AI coding agents</strong> (Claude Code, Codex, OpenHands, and friends) — organized <strong>by security posture first</strong>: how strong the isolation boundary is, and what the agent can still reach beyond it.</p>
</blockquote>

<p>AI coding agents run arbitrary, model-generated commands. The hard part isn’t speed — it’s the <strong>security boundary</strong> (isolation) and what the agent can still do through it (<strong>network egress, secrets</strong>), plus <strong>durable workspace state</strong> for long tasks. This list ranks on those, not boot-time benchmarks.</p>

<h2 id="comparison-matrix">Comparison matrix</h2>

<p><strong>Isolation tier:</strong> microVM (own kernel) > gVisor (user-space kernel) > container (shared kernel) > process.
<strong>Egress control</strong> = can outbound network be restricted — NOT whether it <em>has</em> network. <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">deny-default</code> / <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">allowlist</code> / <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">configurable</code> / <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">full-by-default</code> / <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">none</code>.
<strong>Secrets</strong> = <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">brokered</code> (creds kept OUT via proxy) vs <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">env-in</code> (injected). Sorted by isolation tier, then egress strength.
<strong>Abbrev.:</strong> eph = ephemeral · pers = persistent · Prop. = proprietary.</p>

<h2 id="what-the-data-shows">What the data shows</h2>

<p><strong>Restricted-by-default egress is the minority.</strong> Deny-by-default: <strong>Cleanroom, smolvm (smol-machines), Leap0, InstaVM, Mitos, Baponi</strong>; allowlist-default: <strong>Sprites</strong>. Sixteen offer <em>configurable</em> egress (opt-in), and the rest ship open outbound or delegate/none (Modal, Beam, Northflank, Arrakis, Box, Morph, Tensorlake, Novita, Kubernetes Agent Sandbox, OpenHands). <em>Isolation is common; egress control is not.</em></p>

<p><strong>Secrets brokering (creds kept out of the sandbox)</strong> is now a real cluster: Cleanroom, smolvm, Leap0, InstaVM, Mitos, Superserve, Islo, Declaw, Vercel Sandbox, BoxLite, OpenComputer, Blaxel, microsandbox, Runloop, Baponi, OpenSandbox, Cloudflare, Daytona. Env-in: AgentENV, E2B, Modal, Northflank, Beam, Arrakis, SmolVM (Celesto), Qbox, Katakate, Sprites, Morph, Tensorlake, Box, Novita, AIO Sandbox, Kubernetes Agent Sandbox, OpenHands, OmniRun.</p>

<p><strong>The strong-posture set</strong> (µVM/VM <strong>and</strong> restricted egress <strong>and</strong> brokered secrets) is small: <strong>Cleanroom, smolvm (smol-machines), Leap0, InstaVM, Mitos</strong> — plus Superserve/Islo/Declaw/OpenComputer on configurable egress. That’s the bar to beat.</p>

<p><strong>EU data-residency</strong> is offered by two <em>managed</em> entries — <strong>Box (ascii.dev)</strong> (DE/FI/FR) and <strong>OmniRun</strong> (Hetzner/DE). Self-hostable tools (Mitos, Cleanroom, microsandbox, smolvm, …) can additionally be run in the EU <em>by you</em>. Still a minority across 37 providers.</p>

<p><strong>Control-plane reachable from inside</strong> (the “front desk” risk): Sprites documents an in-sandbox management API (reachable); Modal documents it is <em>not</em>. Others undocumented.</p>

<p><strong>Control-plane authentication:</strong> AgentENV currently has no built-in API authorization. Its maintainers explicitly require deployment on a trusted network or behind an authorization proxy.</p>

<h3 id="how-these-values-were-verified">How these values were verified</h3>

<p>Every cell traces back to the project’s own documentation or source repository — not to blog posts, not to vendor comparisons, not to an earlier revision of this list. Where a project documents nothing, the cell says <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">?</code> rather than a guess: an honest gap is more useful than a confident error. Contributors quote the supporting phrase in the pull request so a reviewer can check the claim without repeating the research, and the matrix is the single source for <a href="https://github.com/fhiltscher/awesome-ai-coding-sandboxes/blob/main/_data/sandboxes.json"><code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">_data/sandboxes.json</code></a>, which CI regenerates and diffs on every change — the structured data this page publishes cannot silently drift from the table above.</p>

<h3 id="what-this-ranking-does-not-measure">What this ranking does not measure</h3>

<p>It reads documentation, not implementations. A <strong>deny-default</strong> cell means the project <em>documents</em> deny-by-default egress; it is not the result of a penetration test, and no escape research was done for this list. Cold-start latency, throughput, pricing, SDK ergonomics and language coverage are deliberately absent — they are covered well elsewhere, and they are not what fails when an agent gets prompt-injected.</p>

<p>A strong row also does not equal a safe deployment. Brokered secrets still require the broker to be configured; an allowlist is only as tight as its entries; a µVM with a mounted host directory has traded its boundary away. Read the matrix as a shortlist filter, then read the docs of the two or three candidates that survive it.</p>

<h2 id="why-security-posture-first">Why security-posture-first</h2>

<p>Community consensus (HN, Reddit, the security literature) is blunt: <strong>containers are not a trust boundary</strong> for untrusted agent code, and <strong>isolation alone “solves the easiest problem”</strong> — the real risk is an agent with legitimate access exfiltrating data via network egress or leaked credentials (prompt injection). So we rank on the boundary <em>and</em> what crosses it, not on cold-start milliseconds (which matter only for ephemeral/high-concurrency workloads, not long-running coding agents).</p>

<p>Key nuance: almost every sandbox <em>has</em> outbound network — that’s the problem, not a feature. The differentiator is whether egress can be <strong>default-denied and allowlisted</strong>, and whether <strong>secrets are brokered so the sandbox never holds them</strong>. A strong microVM with unrestricted network still lets a prompt-injected agent phone home with your code — isolation and egress control are <strong>orthogonal</strong>.</p>

<h2 id="process--namespace-sandboxes">Process & namespace sandboxes</h2>

<p>Syscall/filesystem/network restriction for individual processes, built on Bubblewrap, Landlock, and seccomp.</p>

<ul>
  <li><a href="https://github.com/anthropic-experimental/sandbox-runtime">Anthropic Sandbox Runtime</a> - Filesystem and network restrictions for arbitrary processes via Seatbelt on macOS and bubblewrap on Linux, plus proxy-based domain allowlisting.</li>
  <li><a href="https://github.com/NVIDIA/OpenShell">NVIDIA OpenShell</a> - Agent runtime that enforces declarative YAML policies on file access, exfiltration and network activity (alpha).</li>
  <li><a href="https://github.com/GreyhavenHQ/greywall">Greywall</a> - Container-free, deny-by-default sandbox for filesystem, network and syscalls on Linux and macOS, with an allow-by-default watch mode.</li>
  <li><a href="https://github.com/fencesandbox/fence">Fence</a> - Lightweight, container-free sandbox that runs commands under network and filesystem restrictions.</li>
  <li><a href="https://github.com/Zouuup/landrun">Landrun</a> - Runs any Linux process in an unprivileged Landlock sandbox, firejail-style but kernel-native.</li>
  <li><a href="https://github.com/multikernel/sandlock">sandlock</a> - Confines untrusted code with Landlock, seccomp-bpf and seccomp user notification; no root, no cgroups, copy-on-write working directory.</li>
  <li><a href="https://github.com/TetiAI/hivebox">HiveBox</a> - Namespaces, cgroups, seccomp and Landlock behind a CLI and REST API, one OpenCode agent per sandbox.</li>
  <li><a href="https://github.com/PACHAKUTlQ/ClaudeCage">ClaudeCage</a> - Packs Claude Code into a single portable bubblewrap sandbox scoped to one project directory.</li>
</ul>
